ribe.name: Ribe
ribe.summary: A town in southwestern Jutland, Denmark, and the country's oldest town, seat of the Diocese of Ribe.

birka.name: Birka
birka.summary: A Viking Age trading centre on the island of Björkö in Sweden, flourishing from about 750 to 975 CE and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

oseberg-ship.name: Oseberg Ship burial
oseberg-ship.summary: A well-preserved Viking longship found in a Norwegian burial mound, among the finest surviving Viking Age artifacts, buried no earlier than 834 with a woman thought to be a queen or priestess.

harald-bluetooth.name: Harald Bluetooth
harald-bluetooth.summary: King of Denmark and Norway (r. c. 958-986), son of Gorm the Old and Thyra; his own son Swein Forkbeard forced him from the throne shortly before his death.

jelling-stones.name: Jelling stones
jelling-stones.summary: Two massive 10th-century runestones at Jelling, Denmark; the older honors King Gorm the Old's wife, the larger celebrates his son Harald Bluetooth's conquests and his Christianizing of the Danes. Since 1994 part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

borre-mound-cemetery.name: Borre mound cemetery
borre-mound-cemetery.summary: A Norwegian burial ground with seven large and 21 smaller mounds, the oldest dating to 600 AD, predating the Viking Age.

gamla-uppsala.name: Gamla Uppsala
gamla-uppsala.summary: A village near Uppsala, Sweden, that was a major religious and political center from the 3rd century CE, seat of the legendary Yngling kings and site of the assembly of all Swedes.

lindholm-h-je.name: Lindholm Høje
lindholm-h-je.summary: A major Viking burial site and former settlement overlooking the Danish city of Aalborg.

jelling.name: Jelling
jelling.summary: A Danish railway town of about 4,000 people, roughly 10 km northwest of Vejle.

ansgar.name: Ansgar
ansgar.summary: Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen (801–865) known as the 'Apostle of the North' for his missionary travels bringing Christianity to Northern Europe.

hedeby.name: Hedeby
hedeby.summary: A major Danish Viking Age trading settlement (8th to 11th centuries) near the southern Jutland Peninsula, described by a 10th-century visitor as "a very large city"; abandoned after being destroyed in 1066.

battle-of-svolder.name: Battle of Svolder
battle-of-svolder.summary: A naval battle fought in September 1000 in the western Baltic Sea, in which King Olaf of Norway was defeated by an alliance of the kings of Denmark and Sweden and his Norwegian enemies, tied to Norway's unification and Christianization.

olaf-tryggvason.name: Olaf Tryggvason
olaf-tryggvason.summary: King of Norway from 995 to 1000 who forcibly promoted Christianity, is said to have founded Trondheim in 997, and died in 1000.

swein-forkbeard.name: Sweyn Forkbeard
swein-forkbeard.summary: King of Denmark from about 986 and briefly King of England from December 1013 until his death in 1014, and father of King Cnut.

olof-sk-tkonung.name: Olof Skötkonung
olof-sk-tkonung.summary: King of Sweden from around 995 to 1022, the first to rule both Swedes and Geats, mint coins, and become a Christian ruler in central Sweden.

eir-kr-h-konarson.name: Eirik Hákonarson
eir-kr-h-konarson.summary: Earl of Lade, Governor of Norway and Earl of Northumbria (960s–1020s) who fought at the Battle of Hjörungavágr and the Battle of Svolder, and helped conquer England for King Cnut.

ormrinn-langi.name: Ormen Lange
ormrinn-langi.summary: A famed Viking longship built for Norwegian King Olaf Tryggvason in the late 990s, the largest and most powerful of its day, with 34 pairs of oars.

haakon-sigurdsson.name: Haakon Sigurdsson
haakon-sigurdsson.summary: De facto ruler of Norway from about 975 to 995, also known as Haakon Jarl, and called Haakon the Powerful by some or, less flatteringly, Haakon the Bad.

battle-of-hj-rungav-gr.name: Battle of Hjörungavágr
battle-of-hj-rungav-gr.summary: A semi-legendary late 10th-century naval battle, traditionally dated 986, in which the Jarls of Lade defeated a Danish fleet of Jomsvikings, helping Haakon Sigurdsson unite Norway.

snorri-sturluson.name: Snorri Sturluson
snorri-sturluson.summary: An Icelandic historian, poet and politician (1179–1241) credited with the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, key sources on Norse mythology and kings; he was assassinated in 1241.

harald-fairhair.name: Harald Fairhair
harald-fairhair.summary: Traditionally considered the first King of Norway (reigned c. 872–930), later becoming a national icon of Norwegian unity, though some modern historians doubt he actually existed.

hedmark.name: Hedmark (Hedemark)
hedmark.summary: A former county in eastern Norway bordering Sweden, an agricultural and forestry region merged into Innlandet county in 2020.

gudbrandsdalen.name: Gudbrandsdalen
gudbrandsdalen.summary: A long valley in Norway running northwest from near Lillehammer, associated with early Norwegian kings such as Harald Fairhair.

varangians.name: Varangians
varangians.summary: Viking traders, warriors and settlers, mostly from Sweden, who founded the state of Kievan Rus' and other principalities from the 8th-9th centuries.

varangian-guard.name: Varangian Guard
varangian-guard.summary: An elite bodyguard unit of the Byzantine emperors, mainly composed of Norse and later Anglo-Saxon warriors, formally established under Emperor Basil II in 988.

earls-of-lade.name: Jarls of Lade
earls-of-lade.summary: A dynasty of Norse jarls who ruled Trøndelag and Hålogaland, in what is now Norway, from the 9th to the 11th century, seated near Trondheim.

ingjald.name: Ingjald Illråde
ingjald.summary: A semi-legendary Swedish king of the House of Ynglings, said to have reigned around the 7th century and known mainly through later medieval sagas of uncertain historical accuracy.

granmar.name: Granmar
granmar.summary: A legendary king of Södermanland described in Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla and in the Volsunga saga and Poetic Edda, married to Hilda, daughter of a Geatish king.

s-dermanland.name: Södermanland
s-dermanland.summary: A historical province on Sweden's southeastern coast, bordering Östergötland, Närke, Västmanland and Uppland, and bounded by Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea.

anglo-saxon-chronicle.name: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
anglo-saxon-chronicle.summary: A set of Old English annals on Anglo-Saxon history, first compiled in the late 800s under King Alfred the Great and copied and updated at English monasteries until 1154; its oldest surviving manuscript, held at Cambridge, is called the Parker Chronicle.

edmund-i.name: Edmund I
edmund-i.summary: King of the English from 939 to 946, grandson of Alfred the Great, who recovered territory lost to Viking rulers before being killed in a brawl at age 25.

danelaw.name: Danelaw
danelaw.summary: The part of England under Danish law from the late 9th century to the Norman Conquest, set up after Viking conquest and defined in treaties following Alfred the Great's victory over Guthrum.

adam-of-bremen.name: Adam of Bremen
adam-of-bremen.summary: German medieval chronicler (before 1050 – 1081/1085) known for his history of the Hamburg church, and the first European to write about the New World, mentioning the Norse outpost of Vinland.

snorri-go-i.name: Snorri Goði
snorri-go-i.summary: A powerful 10th- and 11th-century chieftain in western Iceland, remembered in the sagas as unusually shrewd, far-sighted and vengeful.

poetic-edda.name: Poetic Edda
poetic-edda.summary: A collection of anonymous Old Norse poems in alliterative verse, based on the medieval Icelandic Codex Regius manuscript, central to the study of Norse mythology.

skald.name: Skald
skald.summary: A poet who composed skaldic poetry, an ornate form of Old Norse verse using kennings, often to honor Viking-era kings.

younger-futhark.name: Younger Futhark
younger-futhark.summary: A 16-character runic alphabet in use from around the 9th century, a reduced form of the older Elder Futhark used through the Viking Age.

procopius.name: Procopius
procopius.summary: A Greek historian from Caesarea, about 500 to 565, who accompanied the Byzantine general Belisarius and became the principal historian of Emperor Justinian's era.

geats.name: Geats
geats.summary: A North Germanic tribe who inhabited Götaland in southern Sweden from antiquity to the late Middle Ages, ancestors of modern Swedes.

r-k-runestone.name: Rök runestone
r-k-runestone.summary: A Swedish runestone bearing the longest known runic inscription in stone, considered the earliest known work of Swedish literature.

sagas-of-icelanders.name: Sagas of Icelanders
sagas-of-icelanders.summary: A group of Old Icelandic prose narratives, mostly based on real events in Iceland's ninth to eleventh centuries and recorded in the 13th and 14th centuries; the best-known works of Icelandic literature.

proto-norse-language.name: Proto-Norse
proto-norse-language.summary: An early North Germanic language spoken in Scandinavia from about the 2nd to 8th centuries CE, recorded in the oldest Elder Futhark runic inscriptions, evolving into Old Norse around 800 CE.

old-norse.name: Old Norse
old-norse.summary: A North Germanic language spoken in Scandinavia and Norse settlements from about the 8th to 14th centuries, ancestor of Icelandic, Norwegian, Danish and Swedish.

heruli.name: Heruli
heruli.summary: A smaller Germanic people of Late Antiquity who founded a kingdom near the Middle Danube after Attila's empire fell, later scattering to Scandinavia and the Balkans after conquest by the Lombards.

warini.name: Warini
warini.summary: A Germanic people or peoples originally living near the Baltic and North Seas in what is now northern Germany, first mentioned by Roman authors in the first century AD.

odin.name: Odin
odin.summary: A widely revered god of Norse mythology and Germanic paganism, associated with wisdom, poetry and frenzy, worshipped from Roman-era Germania through the Viking Age.

asgard.name: Asgard
asgard.summary: In Norse mythology, the fortified home of the Aesir gods described in the Eddas and other Old Norse texts, roughly equivalent to Mount Olympus in Greek myth.

ahmad-ibn-fadlan.name: Ahmad ibn Fadlan
ahmad-ibn-fadlan.summary: Tenth-century Arab traveler from Baghdad whose account of an Abbasid embassy to the Volga Bulgars famously describes the Volga Vikings, including an eyewitness ship burial.

rus-people.name: Rus'
rus-people.summary: An early medieval people, generally held to be Norsemen mainly from Sweden, who settled and ruled trade routes between the Baltic and Black Sea from the 8th to 11th centuries and gave their name to Russia.

staveless-runes.name: Hälsinge runes
staveless-runes.summary: A simplified runic alphabet, also called staveless runes, that dropped vertical strokes from the Younger Futhark; named for runestones found in Hälsingland.

jordanes.name: Jordanes
jordanes.summary: 6th-century Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent turned historian, whose Getica is one of only two surviving ancient works on early Gothic history.

scandza.name: Scandza
scandza.summary: A legendary 'great island' described by the 6th-century historian Jordanes as the ancestral homeland of the Goths, usually identified with Scandinavia.

steinunn-refsd-ttir.name: Steinunn Refsdóttir
steinunn-refsd-ttir.summary: An Icelandic skald active at the end of the 10th century, remembered for two surviving verses taunting the Christian missionary Þangbrandr.

angbrandr.name: Þangbrandr
angbrandr.summary: A missionary sent to Iceland by King Óláfr Tryggvason of Norway to convert its inhabitants to Christianity.

hildr-hr-lfsd-ttir.name: Hildr Hrólfsdóttir
hildr-hr-lfsd-ttir.summary: A 9th-century Norwegian woman and one of the few female skalds whose verses survive, known from Old Norse sagas for a poem pleading for her banished father.

abecedarium-nordmannicum.name: Abecedarium Nordmannicum
abecedarium-nordmannicum.summary: A 9th-century short poem presenting the 16 runes of the Younger Futhark, preserved in the Codex Sangallensis manuscript; its original text was destroyed in the 19th century.

fulda.name: Fulda
fulda.summary: A city in Hesse, Germany, on the river of the same name, and the administrative seat of the Fulda district.

walafrid-strabo.name: Walafrid Strabo
walafrid-strabo.summary: An Alemannic Benedictine monk and theological writer, about 808 to 849, who lived on Reichenau Island in southern Germany.

ulfberht-swords.name: Ulfberht swords
ulfberht-swords.summary: Group of about 170 medieval swords from the 9th to 11th centuries, found mainly in Northern Europe. Their blades are inlaid with the inscription +VLFBERH+T or +VLFBERHT+, a Frankish personal name.

fennoscandia.name: Fennoscandia
fennoscandia.summary: Peninsula in northern Europe encompassing the Scandinavian and Kola peninsulas, mainland Finland, and Karelia.

schlei.name: Schlei
schlei.summary: Narrow inlet of the Baltic Sea in northern Germany, about 20 miles long, reaching the town of Schleswig. The Viking settlement of Hedeby stood at its head before being abandoned for Schleswig.

eider-river.name: Eider
eider-river.summary: Longest river on the Jutland Peninsula, flowing across Germany's Schleswig-Holstein to the North Sea. From about 800 to 1200 it marked the border between Saxons and Slavs to the south and Danes to the north.

corduroy-road.name: Corduroy road
corduroy-road.summary: Road made by laying logs across the direction of travel over low or swampy ground. It beats mud or dirt, but it is rough, and shifting logs can endanger horses.

uppland.name: Uppland
uppland.summary: A historical Swedish province north of Stockholm, famous for the highest concentration of runestones in the world and home to Sweden's oldest town and university.

dendrochronology.name: Dendrochronology
dendrochronology.summary: The scientific method of dating tree rings to the exact year they formed, useful for precise dating too recent for radiocarbon methods and for calibrating them.

franks.name: Franks
franks.summary: Western European people who began in the third century as Germanic tribes near the Lower Rhine. They gradually became a Catholic Christian people controlling a large territory inside and outside the former Roman Empire.

birka-grave-bj-581.name: Birka grave Bj 581
birka-grave-bj-581.summary: 10th-century Norse burial at Birka, Sweden, holding a woman buried with two horses and an arsenal of weapons. Whether she was a professional warrior is disputed, since grave goods may not show a person's role.

anders-winroth.name: Anders Winroth
anders-winroth.summary: A Swedish medievalist, born 1965, who has taught at the University of Oslo and previously at Yale University.

althing.name: Althing
althing.summary: Iceland's national legislature, founded in 930 at Þingvellir and considered the oldest legislature in the world.

thorgeir-ljosvetningagodi.name: Thorgeir Ljósvetningagoði
thorgeir-ljosvetningagodi.summary: An Icelandic lawspeaker and pagan chieftain who in 999 or 1000 decided that Iceland should adopt Christianity, averting civil conflict between pagans and Christians.

bj-rn-at-haugi.name: Björn
bj-rn-at-haugi.summary: A Swedish king named in the Hervarar saga, sometimes identified with the historically attested Björn mentioned in the 9th-century Vita Ansgarii as a local ruler.

north-sea-empire.name: North Sea Empire
north-sea-empire.summary: Personal union of England, Denmark and Norway under Norse kings for most of 1013 to 1042; at its height under Cnut the Great it was the most powerful realm in western Europe after the Holy Roman Empire.

unni-bishop.name: Unni
unni-bishop.summary: Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen from 916 to 936 who died as a missionary in Birka, Sweden, continuing Ansgar's work; venerated as the third Apostle of the North.

v-sterg-tland.name: Västergötland
v-sterg-tland.summary: One of Sweden's traditional provinces, in the southwest of the country, home to the city of Gothenburg.

olaf-haraldsson.name: Saint Olaf
olaf-haraldsson.summary: King of Norway from 1015 to 1028, canonized as a saint after his death in the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030; his sainthood spread Christianity among Scandinavia's Vikings.

h-vam-l.name: Hávamál
h-vam-l.summary: Old Norse poem attributed to Odin, dated to around 900–1000 CE, offering practical and philosophical wisdom on conduct, plus an account of how Odin won the runes.

norse-cosmology.name: Nine Worlds
norse-cosmology.summary: In Norse cosmology, the nine worlds arranged around the cosmic tree Yggdrasil, part of the ancient North Germanic account of the universe recorded in the Poetic and Prose Eddas.

yggdrasil.name: Yggdrasil
yggdrasil.summary: An immense sacred ash tree at the center of Norse cosmology, described in the 13th-century Poetic and Prose Eddas as supported by three roots and visited daily by the gods.

ymir.name: Ymir
ymir.summary: Primeval being in Norse mythology from whose body the gods Odin, Vili and Vé fashioned the world—earth from his flesh, oceans from his blood, mountains from his bones.

ask-and-embla.name: Ask and Embla
ask-and-embla.summary: The first man and woman in Norse mythology, created and given gifts by three gods, including Odin, according to the Poetic and Prose Eddas.

ragnar-k.name: Ragnarök
ragnar-k.summary: In Norse mythology, a foretold battle in which major gods including Odin, Thor and Loki perish amid catastrophic disasters, after which the world is reborn and two human survivors repopulate it.

til-rs-ok-fri-ar.name: Til árs ok friðar
til-rs-ok-fri-ar.summary: An Old Norse ritual phrase meaning 'for a good year and peace,' used at pagan feasts and later carried into Christian-era Scandinavian law.

bl-t.name: blót
bl-t.summary: Germanic pagan ceremonies centered on sacrificing an animal and communally eating its meat, tied to a ruler's legitimacy and to securing a good harvest, later banned under Christianity.

freyr.name: Freyr
freyr.summary: A Norse god associated with kingship, peace, fertility and good harvest, especially linked to Sweden and its royal house.

klaus-d-wel.name: Klaus Düwel
klaus-d-wel.summary: German philologist (1935–2020) specializing in Germanic studies, a professor at the University of Göttingen and one of the world's leading experts on Germanic Antiquity.

anders-hultg-rd.name: Anders Hultgård
anders-hultg-rd.summary: A Swedish theologian and religious studies scholar, born 1936, former Chair of Religious History at Uppsala University, specializing in Indo-European religions.

gu-mundur-finnbogason.name: Guðmundur Finnbogason
gu-mundur-finnbogason.summary: Icelandic philosopher (1873–1944) and one of the first Icelandic psychologists, whose work influenced Jean Piaget's development stages model.

sveinbjorn-johnson.name: Sveinbjorn Johnson
sveinbjorn-johnson.summary: Icelandic-born American lawyer, politician and scholar (1883-1946).

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Ancient Greek poet, possibly born around the 8th century BC, traditionally credited as author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, foundational works of Greek literature.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

ship-burial.name: Ship burial
ship-burial.summary: A burial practice in which a ship or boat serves as the tomb or part of the grave goods, notably used by Viking Age Norse peoples.

thrall.name: Thrall
thrall.summary: A slave or serf in Scandinavian lands during the Viking Age, ranked below both freemen and noblemen.

gorm-the-old.name: Gorm the Old
gorm-the-old.summary: Ruler of Denmark from about 936 until his death around 958, reigning from Jelling, where he raised the oldest Jelling stone in honor of his wife.
